title: stackalloc and slicing a large CSV (import scenario)
hook: stackalloc allocates a small buffer on the stack instead of the heap — perfect for parsing one CSV line or token when the size is bounded. Combine with Span to slice fields without allocating strings for every column.

blocks.text: stackalloc T[n] creates a buffer in the current stack frame. In modern C# use Span<char> buffer = stackalloc char[256] for safe bounds. Ideal when max line length is known — CSV row parsing, protocol headers. For unbounded or huge rows, use ArrayPool or stream instead — stack overflow is real if you stackalloc megabytes.

blocks.text: Importing a million-row CSV with string.Split per line allocates two objects per row minimum — gen-0 storm. stackalloc plus span parsing keeps hot buffers off the heap for typical row sizes. Module 14 LOH topic: rows over ~85 KB still need pooled arrays, not stack.

blocks.title: Size bound rule
blocks.body: stackalloc only when you have a proven max size (config limit + validation). Otherwise ArrayPool or streaming.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: stackalloc inside loop with unbounded size. Using string.Split on million-row imports. Forgetting to validate line length before stackalloc.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: cap MaxLineBytes before stackalloc and log rejections — a 10 MB line attempt should never reach the stack. BenchmarkDotNet stackalloc + span walk versus string.Split on a 1M-row fixture quantifies gen-0 savings. Stream with yield return keeps memory flat like Node csv-parse; File.ReadAllLines is the anti-pattern that blows heap on import jobs.

snippet.label: Bounded stackalloc line buffer with length guard
snippet.explanation: Line 1: hard cap before any stackalloc sized from user data. Line 7: reject oversize lines at boundary — prevents stack overflow on malicious CSV.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: stackalloc with user-controlled size inside a loop. File.ReadAllLines for million-row production import. string.Split per row on a hot path. Not validating line length before stackalloc.

interviewTakeaways: stackalloc places a bounded buffer on the stack — no GC for that slab when size is proven safe.
Parse CSV with span walks and list patterns, not Split arrays that allocate per row.
In production, cap MaxLineBytes and stream with yield — reject oversize lines before stackalloc.
60s: stackalloc for bounded lines. Span field walk. ArrayPool for large. record struct rows. Never stackalloc from user size. Stream don't ReadAllLines.
Follow-up: when does stackalloc in a loop become a stack overflow risk?
commonPitfalls: stackalloc size tied to user input without cap gets you rejected — hard MaxLineBytes first.
Materializing entire CSV with File.ReadAllLines on production import jobs.
Strong answer: 'Cap line size. stackalloc under cap. Span parse fields. ArrayPool above cap. record struct per row. BenchmarkDotNet Split vs span.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: Node csv-parse streams rows. C# combines StreamReader, span parsing, and yield return for similar streaming without loading all lines.

Parsing CSV in Node often uses Buffer slices without new strings — same as ReadOnlySpan<char> over a rented byte buffer. C# stackalloc is the stack analogue of a fixed-size scratch Buffer.allocUnsafe when max line is bounded.
